title: U.S. Copper Imports Hit 12-Year Record as Tariff Bet Drains Global Stockpiles
excerpt: More than 200,000 tons of copper arrived at American ports in July, the highest monthly volume since at least 2014, while LME inventories outside the U.S. plunge to five-month lows.
body:
• More than 200,000 metric tons of copper arrived at U.S. ports in July, the largest monthly inflow on record in IHS Markit shipping data going back to 2014.
  • Combined Comex and LME inventories in the U.S. now exceed 740,000 tons, with the total American copper hoard estimated at well above 1 million tons.
  • LME warehouse stocks outside the U.S. have fallen sharply as traders divert metal to capture the Comex-LME arbitrage, which averaged more than $350 per ton in July.
  • The import surge continues despite a missed June 30 deadline for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's tariff recommendation, as traders bet the White House will eventually impose duties on refined copper.

A Record Month

Copper is pouring into the United States at the fastest rate in at least 12 years. More than 200,000 metric tons arrived at U.S. ports in July, the biggest monthly inflow on record in IHS Markit shipping data going back to 2014, according to Bloomberg.

The import surge has pushed combined Comex and London Metal Exchange inventories past 740,000 tons, with LME data showing another 110,860 tons sitting in private storage at U.S. ports. The total American copper hoard is now widely estimated at well above 1 million tons — a fivefold increase from under 100,000 metric tons at the start of 2025.

Official Comex inventories have climbed more than 40% this year to a record, driven by traders positioning ahead of President Donald Trump's decision on tariffs for refined copper imports.

The Arbitrage Engine

The trade flows are being driven by a persistent premium for delivering copper to U.S. warehouses. The Comex-LME arbitrage — the spread between front-month Comex copper and the LME cash contract — averaged more than $350 per metric ton in July, comfortably high enough to attract metal from overseas.

"The tariff arbitrage is ruling the roost over demand growth. Those that are closer to whomever is making the formal decision believe they will be better off by bringing more copper into the US today rather than tomorrow."

— Michael Cuoco, Head of Metals, StoneX Financial

The flows have accelerated even after a June 30 deadline for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to recommend action on tariffs passed without an announcement. Last July, Trump directed Lutnick to study whether refined copper imports should face phased tariffs beginning at 15% in January 2027. A decision to impose tariffs on raw metal would likely trigger one final rush of shipments before the levies take effect.

Global Squeeze Tightens

The American import binge is creating a two-speed copper market. While U.S. stockpiles swell, inventories in LME warehouses outside the U.S. have fallen sharply this year as traders diverted metal to American ports.

In the latest sign that the London market is tightening, prices moved to a steeper backwardation — a structure where nearby contracts trade at a premium to futures, signaling short-term supply tightness. Nearby LME contracts traded at a premium of about $99.50 per ton over three-month futures in early August, up from about $30 a week earlier and the widest since January.

Copper topped $14,000 per ton on the LME in early August, its highest level in two months. The metal has rallied about 12% in 2026, aided by speculation about U.S. trade policy and enthusiasm about demand from the energy transition and AI infrastructure buildout.

Supporters and Critics

The tariff debate has divided the copper industry. Supporters argue that levies would encourage investment in domestic mining and processing at a time when the U.S. depends heavily on imports — refined copper currently carries an exemption from Section 232 tariffs, though semi-finished copper products face a 50% duty.

Opponents counter that tariffs on raw metal would raise costs for manufacturers, from wire makers to electric vehicle producers, and make U.S.-made products less competitive globally. The irony is not lost on market observers: the tariff investigation was launched because of U.S. import dependency, but the investigation itself has generated the largest copper import surge in over a decade.

Chinese fabricators, meanwhile, have been buying hand-to-mouth this year, keeping inventories low and sending some LME-stored metal back to China. The competing regional demand signals — U.S. oversupply versus Chinese tightness — are creating a bifurcated global market where price dynamics in one region can amplify scarcity in another.

A decision to abandon the tariff proposal entirely could reverse trade flows as merchants unwind positions accumulated over the past 18 months, potentially flooding the global market with copper trapped in American warehouses.
